segments.speaker: KATIE
segments.en: Joe, you know I’m giving a presentation in our film studies class next week?

segments.speaker: JOE
segments.en: Yes.

segments.speaker: KATIE
segments.en: Well, could we discuss it? I could do with getting someone else’s opinion.

segments.speaker: JOE
segments.en: Of course, Katie. What are you going to talk about?

segments.speaker: KATIE
segments.en: It’s about film adaptations of Shakespeare’s plays. I’ve got very interested in all the different approaches that film directors take.

segments.speaker: JOE
segments.en: Uhuh.

segments.speaker: KATIE
segments.en: So I thought I’d start with Giannetti, who’s professor of film and literature, and in one of his books he came up with a straightforward classification of film adaptations based on how faithful they are to the original plays and novels. [[ ]]

segments.speaker: JOE
segments.en: Right.

segments.speaker: KATIE
segments.en: I’ve already made some notes on that, so I just need to sort those out before the presentation. I thought that next I’d ask the class to come up with the worst examples of Shakespeare adaptations that they’ve seen, and to say why [[ ]] . That should be more fun than having their favourite versions.

segments.speaker: JOE
segments.en: Yes, I can certainly think of a couple!

segments.speaker: KATIE
segments.en: Right. Next I want to talk about Rachel Malchow. I came across something on the internet about her work on film adaptations, and I was thinking of showing some film clips to illustrate her ideas.

segments.speaker: JOE
segments.en: Will you have enough time, though? Both to prepare and during the presentation? After all, I doubt if you’ll be able to find all the clips you want.

segments.speaker: KATIE
segments.en: Hmm. Perhaps you’re right. OK, well, I’d better do some slides instead, saying how various films relate to what she says [[ ]] . That should encourage discussion.

segments.speaker: JOE
segments.en: Mmm.

segments.speaker: KATIE
segments.en: Next I want to say something about how plays may be chosen for adaptation because they’re concerned with issues of the time when the film is made. [[ ]]

segments.speaker: JOE
segments.en: You mean things like patriotism, or the role of governments?

segments.speaker: KATIE
segments.en: Exactly. It’s quite tricky, but I’ve got a few ideas I’d like to discuss. ———————–

segments.speaker: KATIE
segments.en: And finally I want to talk about a few adaptations that I think illustrate a range of approaches, and make some comments on them. Do you know the Japanese film Ran?

segments.speaker: JOE
segments.en: I haven’t seen it. It was based on Shakespeare’s King Lear, wasn’t it?

segments.speaker: KATIE
segments.en: That’s right. It was a very loose adaptation, using the same situation and story, but moving it to 16th century Japan instead of 16th century Britain [[ ]] . So for example the king’s daughters become sons, because in Japanese culture at that time, women couldn’t succeed to the throne.

segments.speaker: JOE
segments.en: OK. I hope you’re going to talk about the 1993 film of Much Ado About Nothing. I think that’s one of the best Shakespeare films. It really brings the play to life, doesn’t it?

segments.speaker: KATIE
segments.en: Yes, I agree. And I think filming it in Italy, where the play is set, makes you see what life was like at the time of the play. [[ ]]

segments.speaker: JOE
segments.en: Absolutely. Right, what’s next?

segments.speaker: KATIE
segments.en: Er, next, I thought Romeo & Juliet, the 1996 film, which moves the action into the present day. [[ ]]

segments.speaker: JOE
segments.en: Yes, it worked really well, I thought – changing the two feuding families in the original to two competing business empires, even though they’re speaking in the English of the original play.

segments.speaker: KATIE
segments.en: You’d expect it would sound really bizarre, but I found I soon got used to it.

segments.speaker: JOE
segments.en: Me too.

segments.speaker: KATIE
segments.en: Then I thought I’d include a real Hollywood film, one that’s intended to appeal to a mass commercial audience.

segments.speaker: JOE
segments.en: There must be quite a number of those.

segments.speaker: KATIE
segments.en: Yes, but I’ve picked the 1996 film of Hamlet. It included every line of the text, but it’s more like a typical action hero movie [[ ]] – there are loads of special effects, but no unifying interpretation of the play.

segments.speaker: JOE
segments.en: All show and no substance.

segments.speaker: KATIE
segments.en: Exactly. Then there’s Prospero’s Books, based on The Tempest. That was really innovative, from a stylistic point of view. [[ ]]

segments.speaker: JOE
segments.en: Didn’t it include dance and singing and animation, as well as live actors?

segments.speaker: KATIE
segments.en: Yes, it did. I also want to mention Looking for Richard. Did you ever see it? [[ ]]

segments.speaker: JOE
segments.en: No, but I’ve read about it. It was a blend of a documentary with a few scenes from Richard III, wasn’t it?

segments.speaker: KATIE
segments.en: That’s right. It’s more a way of looking into how people nowadays connect with the playwright – the play is really just the starting point. And that’ll be where I finish.

segments.speaker: JOE
segments.en: Well, it sounds as though it’ll be very interesting.
